description: Green plants: green algae, mosses, ferns, conifers and flowering plants, with a focus on fruits, vegetables and crops and the wild ancestors (and hybrid crosses) they came from.

nodes.name: Chlorophyte green algae
nodes.summary: The 'classic' green algae of ponds, puddles and oceans, from single swimming cells to seaweeds. They are cousins of land plants, not their ancestors.
facts: Sea lettuce, a chlorophyte seaweed, is eaten in salads and soups around the world.
Many lichens are partnerships between a fungus and a chlorophyte alga, and a green alga even grows in sloth fur.

nodes.name: Chlamydomonas
nodes.summary: A single green cell that swims with two whip-like flagella and steers toward light using a red eyespot. Biologists use it as a 'lab rat' for studying photosynthesis and flagella.
facts: A light-sensing protein from Chlamydomonas, channelrhodopsin, launched optogenetics: switching brain cells on and off with flashes of light.
It snows red in some mountains in summer because of related snow algae.

nodes.name: Volvox
nodes.summary: Hollow, spinning green balls made of up to 50,000 cells working together. Volvox is a living example of how single cells can team up into a multicellular body.
facts: Baby colonies grow inside the parent ball, then turn themselves inside out before hatching.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek described Volvox in 1700, peering through his homemade microscope.

nodes.name: Streptophytes
nodes.summary: The branch of green life that includes some freshwater algae and every land plant. Their algae ancestors already had tricks that later helped plants survive on dry land.

nodes.name: Stoneworts
nodes.summary: Freshwater algae that look surprisingly like little plants, with stems and whorls of branches. Many coat themselves in crunchy lime, which gives them their name.
facts: Chara is nicknamed 'muskgrass' because it smells musky, a bit like garlic or skunk.
Their limey crusts build up into lake-bottom sediments and even fossils over 400 million years old.

nodes.name: Conjugating green algae
nodes.summary: Simple green threads and single cells such as Spirogyra, with spiral ribbon-shaped chloroplasts. DNA studies show they are the closest living relatives of all land plants.
facts: Surprisingly, the closest algal cousins of trees and flowers are these slimy pond threads, not the more plant-like stoneworts.
They mate by building a tube between two filaments and sliding one cell's contents across: 'conjugation'.

nodes.name: Land plants
nodes.summary: Plants that left the water and turned bare rock into green land. They protect their baby plant (the embryo) inside the parent, which is where the name Embryophyta comes from.
facts: The oldest fossil spores of land plants are about 470 million years old, but DNA clocks hint they may be older still.
Early land plants teamed up with fungi to get water and nutrients from rock, a partnership most plants still rely on.
By weathering rocks and pulling carbon dioxide from the air, early land plants may have helped trigger an ice age.

nodes.name: Liverworts
nodes.summary: Small, flat or leafy plants that hug damp ground. With no roots or water pipes, they are among the simplest land plants alive.
facts: Their name comes from the old belief that liver-shaped plants could cure liver illnesses.
Some grow tiny 'splash cups': raindrops knock out little clones that grow into new plants.

nodes.name: Mosses
nodes.summary: Soft green cushions made of tiny leafy stems. Mosses have no true roots and can dry out completely, then spring back to life when it rains.
facts: Moss frozen under Antarctic ice for over 1,500 years started growing again when scientists thawed it.
There are roughly 12,000 species of moss.

nodes.name: Peat moss
nodes.summary: Sphagnum moss builds bogs: it soaks up water like a sponge and makes its surroundings acidic, so dead plants pile up as peat instead of rotting.
facts: Sphagnum can hold up to about 20 times its own dry weight in water and was used as wound dressing in World War I.
Peatlands cover only about 3% of the land but store more carbon than all other kinds of vegetation in the world combined.
The acidic bogs it creates have preserved 'bog bodies', people who died thousands of years ago, with skin and hair intact.

nodes.name: Hornworts
nodes.summary: Flat green plants that send up little horn-shaped spore stalks. They are small and easy to overlook, yet hold clues to how the first land plants lived.
facts: Hornworts keep nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria inside slimy pockets, a built-in fertiliser factory.
Their cells contain an algae-like carbon-concentrating structure that no other land plants have.

nodes.name: Vascular plants
nodes.summary: Plants with internal plumbing: xylem pipes carry water up and phloem carries sugar around. Stiffened with lignin, they could finally grow tall.
facts: Lignin, the tough stuff in wood, is so hard to break down that for millions of years few microbes could digest it.
Almost every plant you can name, from ferns to oak trees to grass, is a vascular plant.

nodes.name: Cooksonia
nodes.summary: One of the earliest known upright land plants: forked green stems a few centimetres tall, topped with spore capsules. It had no leaves and no roots.
facts: Most Cooksonia were shorter than your little finger.
It is named after Australian botanist Isabel Cookson.

nodes.name: Lycophytes
nodes.summary: Clubmosses, spikemosses and quillworts: the oldest surviving branch of vascular plants. Today they are small, but their ancestors were giant trees.

nodes.name: Lepidodendron
nodes.summary: A giant 'scale tree' of the Carboniferous coal swamps, growing to 30 metres or more. Its trunk was covered in diamond-shaped leaf scars like reptile skin.
facts: Much of the coal burned since the Industrial Revolution formed from the buried remains of scale trees like Lepidodendron.
It was a relative of today's tiny clubmosses, not of modern trees.
Fossil trunk pieces have been mistaken for the skin of giant snakes or lizards.

nodes.name: Clubmosses
nodes.summary: Small evergreen plants that look like mossy miniature pine trees. They are the living cousins of the giant coal-swamp lycopsids.
facts: Clubmoss spores, called lycopodium powder, burst into a bright flash when blown into a flame and were used in early flash photography and stage magic.

nodes.name: Euphyllophytes
nodes.summary: The plants with true, broad leaves: ferns, horsetails and all seed plants. Their leaves evolved from flattened, webbed branches.

nodes.name: Ferns
nodes.summary: Feathery-leaved plants that spread by spores instead of seeds. New fronds uncurl from tight spirals called fiddleheads.
facts: A small fern from New Caledonia, Tmesipteris oblanceolata, has the largest genome known: about 50 times bigger than yours.
Victorian Britain had a 'fern craze' called pteridomania, with fern patterns on everything from teapots to gravestones.
There are about 10,500 species of ferns alive today.

nodes.name: Horsetails
nodes.summary: Jointed, hollow-stemmed plants that look like green bottlebrushes. Equisetum is the last survivor of a group that once included tree-sized Calamites.
facts: Their stems are full of silica, so people once used them to scrub pots: they're also called 'scouring rush'.
Horsetails have barely changed for over 100 million years, making them true 'living fossils'.

nodes.name: Mosquito fern
nodes.summary: A tiny floating fern that partners with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria living inside its leaves. It can double its mass in just a few days.
facts: Farmers in Asia have grown Azolla in rice paddies for centuries as a natural fertiliser.
About 49 million years ago, Azolla blooms covered the Arctic Ocean and may have helped cool the whole planet.

nodes.name: Archaeopteris
nodes.summary: One of the first true trees, with real wood and spreading branches, forming Earth's earliest forests. It still reproduced with spores, not seeds.
facts: Archaeopteris could reach 20–30 metres tall and covered much of the Late Devonian world.
Its wood looked so much like a conifer's that the trunks were first described as a different plant.

nodes.name: Seed plants
nodes.summary: Plants that package their babies in seeds: an embryo, a packed lunch and a protective coat. With pollen instead of swimming sperm, they no longer needed water to reproduce.
facts: The oldest known seeds are about 365 million years old, from West Virginia.
Seeds can wait: sacred lotus seeds about 1,300 years old have sprouted.

nodes.name: Seed ferns
nodes.summary: Extinct plants with fern-like leaves that carried seeds instead of spores. They were common in the coal forests and later.
facts: For decades, people assumed their fossil leaves belonged to ordinary ferns until seeds were found attached.

nodes.name: Glossopteris
nodes.summary: A tongue-leaved seed plant that dominated the cold southern continents of the Permian. It vanished in the great end-Permian extinction.
facts: Its fossils are found in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica, proof that these were once joined as Gondwana.
Captain Scott's doomed Antarctic team hauled about 16 kg of Glossopteris fossils with them to the very end.

nodes.name: Gymnosperms
nodes.summary: 'Naked seed' plants whose seeds sit exposed on cones or scales instead of inside a fruit. They include conifers, cycads, ginkgo and gnetophytes.

nodes.name: Cycads
nodes.summary: Palm-like plants with stiff leaves and big cones, common in the age of dinosaurs. They are not palms at all.
facts: Cycads are among the most endangered plant groups on Earth.
Some cycad cones heat themselves up to attract the insects that pollinate them.
Like ginkgo, cycads still have swimming sperm, a leftover from their water-loving ancestors.

nodes.name: Ginkgo
nodes.summary: The maidenhair tree, last survivor of a group that has existed since before the dinosaurs. Its fan-shaped leaves turn brilliant gold in autumn.
facts: Six ginkgo trees survived the Hiroshima atomic bomb within 2 km of the blast and are still alive.
Female ginkgo seeds smell like rancid butter or vomit because of butyric acid.
Ginkgo pollen makes swimming sperm cells, discovered by a Japanese botanist in 1896.

nodes.name: Conifers
nodes.summary: Cone-bearing trees such as pines, firs, cypresses and sequoias. They hold the records for the tallest, biggest and oldest living trees.
facts: Vast conifer forests of the north, the taiga, form the largest land biome on Earth.

nodes.name: Pine family
nodes.summary: Pines, firs, spruces, larches and cedars. Most have needle leaves and woody cones.
facts: Larches are conifers that drop all their needles every autumn.

nodes.name: Pines
nodes.summary: About 120 species of needle-leaved trees with woody cones, found across the Northern Hemisphere. Their resin seals wounds and once caulked ships.
facts: Pine nuts, eaten in pesto, are the seeds of certain pine species.
Some pine cones only open after a fire has heated them.

nodes.name: Great Basin bristlecone pine
nodes.summary: Gnarled pines of the high, dry mountains of the western USA, and some of the oldest individual living things on Earth.
facts: A tree nicknamed Methuselah, in California's White Mountains, is more than 4,800 years old: it sprouted before the Great Pyramid of Giza was built.
In 1964 a researcher cut down a bristlecone called Prometheus and only afterwards discovered it was about 4,900 years old.

nodes.name: Cypress family
nodes.summary: Cypresses, junipers, redwoods and sequoias. Many have scale-like leaves, and the family includes the tallest and most massive trees on Earth.
facts: Juniper 'berries', used to flavour gin, are really tiny fleshy cones.

nodes.name: Giant sequoia
nodes.summary: The most massive trees on Earth, growing in California's Sierra Nevada. They can live for more than 3,000 years.
facts: The tree General Sherman holds about 1,500 cubic metres of wood, the largest single tree by volume.
Its bark can be over half a metre thick and protects it from forest fires; fire even helps its cones release seeds.
Its close cousin the coast redwood is the tallest tree: Hyperion is about 116 metres high.

nodes.name: Wollemi pine
nodes.summary: A 'dinosaur tree' of the araucaria family, known only from fossils until 1994, when a ranger found a few dozen growing in a hidden canyon near Sydney, Australia.
facts: Fewer than 100 adult trees survive in the wild, at a secret location.
During the 2019–2020 bushfires, firefighters were flown in to protect the last wild grove with sprinklers and fire retardant.
Nurseries now sell Wollemi pines worldwide to help keep the species alive.

nodes.name: Welwitschia
nodes.summary: A bizarre desert plant from Namibia and Angola that grows only two leaves in its entire life, which keep growing and shred into ribbons.
facts: Some Welwitschia plants are estimated to be over 1,000 years old.
It survives in the Namib Desert partly by catching moisture from coastal fog.

nodes.name: Flowering plants
nodes.summary: Plants with flowers and fruits. Teaming up with insects and other animals for pollination and seed dispersal, they exploded into about 300,000 species and now dominate most landscapes.
facts: Almost all of the food humans eat comes, directly or indirectly, from flowering plants.
Charles Darwin called their sudden appearance in the fossil record an 'abominable mystery'.
A fruit is just a ripened ovary: the part of the flower that wraps the seeds.

nodes.name: Amborella
nodes.summary: A small shrub found only on the Pacific island of New Caledonia. It sits on the very first branch of the flowering-plant family tree, sister to all the others.
facts: Its mitochondria hold huge chunks of DNA stolen from other plants, including mosses and green algae.
Studying Amborella helps scientists imagine what the very first flowers were like.

nodes.name: Water lilies
nodes.summary: One of the oldest branches of flowering plants, floating their round leaves on ponds and lakes.
facts: The giant Amazon water lily has leaves up to 3 metres across that can hold the weight of a small child.
Its ribbed leaves inspired the iron-and-glass design of London's Crystal Palace in 1851.
Lotus flowers look like water lilies but are actually closer relatives of plane trees.

nodes.name: Magnoliids
nodes.summary: An early branch of flowering plants including magnolias, laurels, avocado, cinnamon, nutmeg and black pepper.

nodes.name: Magnolias
nodes.summary: Big, waxy, ancient-looking flowers. Magnolias evolved before bees existed and are mostly pollinated by beetles.
facts: Their tough flower parts help them survive clumsy, chewing beetle pollinators.
The genus is named after French botanist Pierre Magnol.

nodes.name: Laurel family
nodes.summary: Aromatic trees and shrubs that give us bay leaves, cinnamon, camphor and avocados.
facts: Ancient Greeks crowned victors with wreaths of bay laurel leaves.

nodes.name: Avocado
nodes.summary: A tree from Mexico and Central America with a huge seed. Its big fruit evolved to be swallowed whole by giant animals that are now extinct.
facts: The avocado is a 'ghost of evolution': its seed was likely spread by giant ground sloths, gomphotheres and other megafauna that vanished about 13,000 years ago.
The word comes from the Aztec (Nahuatl) word āhuacatl.
Avocado leaves, skin and pits contain persin, which is toxic to birds and many pets.
nodes.origin: People in southern Mexico ate wild avocados about 10,000 years ago and began cultivating them several thousand years later; Mesoamerican farmers selected bigger, fleshier fruit.

nodes.name: Hass avocado
nodes.summary: The bumpy, dark-skinned avocado in almost every supermarket. Every single Hass tree is a grafted clone of one seedling from a Californian backyard.
facts: Hass accounts for most avocados eaten worldwide.
The original 'mother tree' lived until 2002, when it died of root rot.
nodes.origin: Grown from a chance seedling by postman Rudolph Hass in La Habra Heights, California, in the 1920s; patented in 1935.

nodes.name: Monocots
nodes.summary: Flowering plants that sprout with a single seed leaf and usually have long leaves with parallel veins. Grasses, palms, orchids, lilies and bananas are monocots.
facts: Rice, wheat, maize, sugarcane, bananas and coconuts are all monocots, so they feed much of humanity.

nodes.name: Asparagales
nodes.summary: A huge order of monocots including orchids, asparagus, onions, garlic, irises, aloe and agave.

nodes.name: Orchids
nodes.summary: One of the two largest plant families, with around 28,000 species and endlessly strange flowers. Many trick insects into pollinating them.
facts: Orchid seeds are as fine as dust and have no food stores; they need a fungus partner to germinate.
Bee orchids grow flowers that look and smell like female bees to lure males.

nodes.name: Vanilla
nodes.summary: A climbing orchid vine from Mexico whose cured seed pods give us vanilla flavour. Each flower opens for just one day.
facts: In 1841 a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion, Edmond Albius, invented the quick hand-pollination method still used today.
Vanilla is the second most expensive spice after saffron, because every flower must be pollinated by hand outside Mexico.
nodes.origin: First cultivated by the Totonac people of eastern Mexico and prized by the Aztecs; hand-pollination, invented in 1841 on Réunion, let it be farmed worldwide.

nodes.name: Onion
nodes.summary: A layered bulb grown and eaten worldwide for thousands of years. No truly wild onion has ever been found: it exists only as a crop.
facts: Cutting an onion releases a gas, syn-propanethial-S-oxide, that stings your eyes and makes you cry.
Ancient Egyptians placed onions in tombs; Pharaoh Ramesses IV was mummified with onions in his eye sockets.
nodes.origin: Probably domesticated in Central Asia at least 5,000–7,000 years ago from wild Allium relatives.

nodes.name: Palms
nodes.summary: About 2,600 species of tropical trees with crowns of big fan or feather leaves. Palm 'trunks' are not true wood and have no growth rings.
facts: The coco de mer palm has the biggest seed in the world, which can weigh more than 15 kg.

nodes.name: Coconut
nodes.summary: A palm whose giant floating seeds can drift across oceans and still sprout. It supplies food, drink, oil, fibre and building material across the tropics.
facts: A coconut is not a true nut but a drupe, like a peach with a fibrous husk instead of juicy flesh.
Portuguese sailors named it 'coco', meaning a grinning goblin face, after the three holes on the shell.
nodes.origin: Cultivated at least twice: once in island Southeast Asia and the Pacific, and once around southern India; Austronesian sailors spread it across the oceans.

nodes.name: Date palm
nodes.summary: A desert palm whose sweet, sticky fruits have fed people in the Middle East and North Africa for thousands of years. Trees are either male or female.
facts: A tree nicknamed Methuselah was grown in 2005 from a roughly 2,000-year-old seed found at Masada in Israel.
Ancient Mesopotamian farmers hand-pollinated dates, one of the earliest examples of deliberate plant breeding.
nodes.origin: Domesticated around the Persian Gulf at least 7,000 years ago; farmers learned to hand-pollinate female trees.

nodes.name: Gingers and bananas
nodes.summary: A tropical order including bananas, ginger, turmeric, cardamom, birds-of-paradise flowers and arrowroot.
facts: Ginger, turmeric and cardamom are all spices from this order.

nodes.name: Bananas
nodes.summary: Giant herbs, not trees: the 'trunk' is a tight roll of leaf bases. Wild bananas are full of hard seeds; the ones we eat are seedless mutants kept alive by people.
facts: Botanically, a banana is a berry.
Bananas are slightly radioactive because they contain potassium-40, a natural isotope.
A banana plant grows its fruit only once, then dies back and new shoots take over.

nodes.name: Wild banana (acuminata)
nodes.summary: A wild banana of Southeast Asia and New Guinea, packed with hard seeds. It is the main ancestor of almost all dessert bananas.
facts: Wild bananas have so many pea-sized seeds that there is very little flesh to eat.
Its genetic letter 'A' appears in banana codes: dessert bananas are 'AAA'.
People in New Guinea were cultivating bananas about 7,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Wild banana (balbisiana)
nodes.summary: A tough, drought-tolerant wild banana from South Asia and southern China. Its 'B' genome adds hardiness and starchiness to plantains and cooking bananas.

nodes.name: Cavendish banana
nodes.summary: The supermarket banana. It is a sterile triploid (three sets of acuminata chromosomes, 'AAA'), so it has no seeds and every plant is a clone grown from a cutting.
facts: Nearly all bananas traded internationally are Cavendish, which makes them all genetically identical.
Because clones can't evolve resistance, a fungus called Tropical Race 4 now threatens Cavendish plantations worldwide.
nodes.origin: Arose from cultivated Musa acuminata in Southeast Asia or southern China; named after the 6th Duke of Devonshire, William Cavendish, whose gardener Joseph Paxton grew it at Chatsworth House, England, in the 1830s.

nodes.name: Gros Michel banana
nodes.summary: 'Big Mike', the creamy, sweeter banana everyone ate until the 1950s. A soil fungus, Panama disease, wiped out the world's export plantations.
facts: Banana companies switched to the Cavendish because it resisted that strain of Panama disease.
Many people say artificial banana flavour tastes more like Gros Michel than like today's bananas.
It is still grown in small farms, so it is rare rather than extinct.
nodes.origin: A seedless 'AAA' clone from Southeast Asia, carried to the Caribbean in the 1830s and grown on vast Central American plantations.

nodes.name: Plantain
nodes.summary: A starchy cooking banana with genomes from both wild species ('AAB'). Fried, boiled or mashed, it is a staple food across Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean.
facts: Plantains are usually cooked, even when ripe and black-skinned.
nodes.origin: Formed when cultivated Musa acuminata crossed with Musa balbisiana in Southeast Asia; reached Africa thousands of years ago, where Central and West Africa became a huge centre of plantain diversity.

nodes.name: Grasses, sedges and bromeliads
nodes.summary: A big order that includes the grasses, sedges, rushes, cattails and the bromeliads such as pineapple.

nodes.name: Pineapple
nodes.summary: A bromeliad from South America. Each pineapple is really 100 or more small fruits fused together around a stem.
facts: In 18th-century Britain pineapples were such luxury items that people rented them to show off at parties.
Pineapple contains bromelain, an enzyme that breaks down proteins, which is why it tingles your tongue.
Europeans named it 'pine apple' because it looked like a pine cone.
nodes.origin: Domesticated by Indigenous peoples of lowland South America, probably around today's Paraguay and southern Brazil; Columbus's crew met it on Guadeloupe in 1493.

nodes.name: Grasses
nodes.summary: About 12,000 species, from lawn grass to bamboo, covering prairies and savannas worldwide. Their seeds, as cereals, built human civilisation.
facts: Rice, wheat and maize alone provide about half of all the calories people eat.
Grass grows from the base of the leaf, so it keeps growing after being grazed or mowed.
Grass fragments found in fossil dinosaur dung from India show that some dinosaurs ate grass.

nodes.name: Bamboo
nodes.summary: Giant woody grasses, some taller than a house. Certain bamboos are the fastest-growing plants on Earth.
facts: Some bamboos can grow nearly a metre in a single day.
Some species flower only once every 100+ years, and all plants of that species bloom at the same time worldwide, then die.
Giant pandas eat 12–38 kg of bamboo every day.

nodes.name: Rices
nodes.summary: The genus of rice plants: about 20 wild species of wet tropical places, plus Asian and African rice.
facts: Rice was domesticated twice: Asian rice in China and African rice along the Niger River.

nodes.name: Wild rice (Oryza rufipogon)
nodes.summary: A wild rice of Asian marshes and riversides. Its grains fall off as soon as they ripen, great for spreading seeds but terrible for harvesting.
facts: Not to be confused with North American 'wild rice', which is a different grass genus, Zizania.

nodes.name: Rice
nodes.summary: The staple food of more than half the people on Earth. Grown in flooded paddies, it was domesticated from wild Oryza rufipogon in China.
facts: A single mutation in a gene called sh4 helped stop rice grains from shattering, so farmers could harvest them.
There are more than 40,000 varieties of rice.
Rice grows on every continent except Antarctica.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in the Yangtze River valley of China around 9,000 years ago; farmers selected plants whose grains stayed on the stalk. Spread across Asia and later the world.

nodes.name: Wheat tribe
nodes.summary: The grass tribe of wheat, barley, rye and goat grasses. These grasses hybridise readily, which is how bread wheat was born.

nodes.name: Goat grasses
nodes.summary: Weedy wild grasses of the Middle East and Central Asia. Two of them donated whole genomes to modern wheat.

nodes.name: Tausch's goat grass
nodes.summary: A scrappy wild grass from around the Caspian Sea. By crossing with farmers' emmer wheat, it became the third parent of bread wheat.
facts: Its 'D' genome gave bread wheat its stretchy, bread-making gluten and its ability to grow in colder climates.

nodes.name: Einkorn wheat
nodes.summary: One of the very first crops ever domesticated: a small, hulled wheat with just one grain per spikelet ('einkorn' means 'one grain').
facts: Ötzi the Iceman, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago, had einkorn in his last meal.
nodes.origin: Domesticated about 10,500 years ago from wild einkorn in the Karacadağ mountains of south-eastern Turkey.

nodes.name: Wild emmer
nodes.summary: A wild wheat of the Fertile Crescent with four sets of chromosomes. It formed naturally when a wild einkorn-like wheat crossed with a goat grass.
facts: Its parents were Triticum urartu and a goat grass close to Aegilops speltoides.
Wild emmer was rediscovered in 1906 growing on a hillside in Galilee by agronomist Aaron Aaronsohn.

nodes.name: Emmer wheat
nodes.summary: The main wheat of the ancient Near East and Egypt, used for bread and beer. Its descendant durum wheat gives us pasta.
facts: Italians still grow emmer and call it farro.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from wild emmer in the Fertile Crescent (south-eastern Turkey and the Levant) about 10,000–10,500 years ago.

nodes.name: Bread wheat
nodes.summary: The world's most widely planted crop. It carries six sets of chromosomes from three different grasses, the result of an accidental cross in an ancient farmer's field.
facts: Its genome is about five times larger than a human's.
Wheat covers more of the world's farmland than any other crop.
nodes.origin: Arose about 8,000–9,000 years ago when farmers' emmer wheat crossed with wild Tausch's goat grass, south-west of the Caspian Sea; spread with farming across Europe and Asia.

nodes.name: Wild barley
nodes.summary: The wild grass of the Fertile Crescent whose shattering ears scatter seeds as soon as they ripen. It is the direct ancestor of barley.

nodes.name: Barley
nodes.summary: One of the first cereals farmed by humans, used for bread, porridge, animal feed and, of course, beer and whisky.
facts: UK and US shoe sizes still go up in steps of one 'barleycorn', an old unit equal to a third of an inch.
Barley was one of the main crops of ancient Egypt, where beer was part of workers' daily rations.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from wild barley in the Fertile Crescent about 10,000 years ago, and possibly again further east.

nodes.name: Tropical tall grasses
nodes.summary: A grass tribe of warm places, with super-efficient C4 photosynthesis. It includes maize, sugarcane and sorghum.

nodes.name: Sugarcane
nodes.summary: A giant grass with sweet, juicy stems. It is the world's biggest crop by weight, harvested at nearly 2 billion tonnes a year.
facts: The word 'sugar' comes from the Sanskrit word śarkarā.
Sugar plantations in the Americas drove the transatlantic slave trade.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from wild Saccharum robustum in New Guinea around 8,000 years ago; people in India first learned to crystallise sugar about 2,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Teosinte
nodes.summary: A bushy wild grass from Mexico with tiny ears of 5–12 rock-hard kernels. It looks so unlike corn that it was once put in a different genus.
facts: Teosinte kernels can be popped like popcorn.
A handful of genes, like teosinte branched1, explain most of the dramatic change from teosinte to maize.

nodes.name: Maize (corn)
nodes.summary: The most produced grain on Earth, bred from scrawny teosinte into ears with hundreds of kernels. Popcorn, sweetcorn and cornflakes all come from it.
facts: Modern maize cannot survive without people: its kernels stay locked on the cob and cannot spread themselves.
Indigenous farmers often grew maize with beans and squash: the 'Three Sisters'.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from Balsas teosinte in the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico about 9,000 years ago; spread across the Americas long before Europeans arrived.

nodes.name: Eudicots
nodes.summary: About three-quarters of all flowering plants, from daisies and roses to oaks and tomatoes. They usually sprout with two seed leaves and have net-veined leaves.
facts: Eudicots are recognised by their pollen grains, which have three grooves.

nodes.name: Caryophyllales
nodes.summary: A surprising order that includes cacti, carnivorous plants, carnations, spinach, quinoa and beets.
facts: Venus flytraps and sundews belong to this order, as do the cacti.
The famous story that spinach's iron was overestimated because of a misplaced decimal point is itself a myth.

nodes.name: Sea beet
nodes.summary: A wild, leafy beet of European seashores. Beetroot, chard, sugar beet and fodder beet are all varieties of this same species.

nodes.name: Beetroot
nodes.summary: A beet bred for its swollen, deep-red root. Ancient people ate beet leaves; fat red roots came much later.
facts: Some people pee pink after eating beetroot, a harmless condition called beeturia.
Its red pigment, betanin, is used to colour foods like strawberry ice cream.
nodes.origin: Leafy beets were grown around the Mediterranean in ancient times; the round red root types were developed in Europe by around the 16th century.

nodes.name: Sugar beet
nodes.summary: A pale beet bred to store sugar in its root. It supplies about a fifth of the world's sugar.
facts: Napoleon promoted sugar beet after British blockades cut France off from Caribbean cane sugar.
nodes.origin: In 1747 German chemist Andreas Marggraf found beet sugar identical to cane sugar; Franz Achard bred high-sugar beets and opened the first beet sugar factory in Silesia in 1801.

nodes.name: Rosids
nodes.summary: A vast branch of eudicots including roses, legumes, citrus, cabbages, melons, grapes, maples and oaks. Many of our favourite fruits are rosids.

nodes.name: Grapevines
nodes.summary: Climbing woody vines that hold on with tendrils. About 70 wild species grow across the Northern Hemisphere.
facts: In the 1860s–1880s a tiny American aphid, phylloxera, destroyed most of Europe's vineyards; they were saved by grafting onto resistant American grape roots.

nodes.name: Wild grapevine
nodes.summary: The wild ancestor of the wine grape, a forest vine from Western Europe to Central Asia. Each wild vine is either male or female.

nodes.name: Grape
nodes.summary: The grapevine of vineyards, table grapes and raisins. Farmers chose rare vines with flowers that were both male and female, so every plant bears fruit.
facts: Grapes are grown from cuttings, so famous varieties are ancient clones; DNA showed that Cabernet Sauvignon came from a chance cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.
The oldest known winery, in a cave in Armenia, is about 6,100 years old.
nodes.origin: Domesticated about 11,000 years ago, at almost the same time in Western Asia and the South Caucasus, first for eating; wine-making grapes were developed as vines spread into Europe.

nodes.name: Legumes
nodes.summary: The bean family: peas, beans, lentils, peanuts, clover and acacias. Bacteria in their root nodules turn nitrogen from the air into natural fertiliser.
facts: With about 20,000 species, it is the third-largest plant family.
Farmers rotate legumes with other crops to enrich the soil with nitrogen.

nodes.name: Pea
nodes.summary: Round green seeds in a pod, one of the 'founder crops' farmed alongside wheat and barley at the dawn of agriculture.
facts: Gregor Mendel discovered the basic rules of heredity by breeding nearly 30,000 pea plants in his monastery garden.
Mendel's 'wrinkled' peas are caused by a jumping gene that broke a starch-making enzyme.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in the Fertile Crescent about 10,000–11,000 years ago from wild Pisum relatives.

nodes.name: Soybean
nodes.summary: A protein-rich bean used for tofu, soy sauce, oil and animal feed. It was domesticated from the wild soybean, a thin twining vine of East Asia.
facts: Most of the world's soybeans are fed to farm animals, not eaten directly by people.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from wild Glycine soja in northern and central China roughly 5,000–9,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Peanut
nodes.summary: Not a nut but a legume. After pollination, the flower stalk bends down and pushes the young pod into the soil, where the peanuts grow.
facts: George Washington Carver promoted hundreds of uses for peanuts, but he did not invent peanut butter.
The two wild parents normally grow hundreds of kilometres apart; people may have carried one to the other.
nodes.origin: Formed in South America from a cross between two wild species, Arachis duranensis and Arachis ipaensis, probably about 10,000 years ago after people brought them together; domesticated in the region of Bolivia and northern Argentina.

nodes.name: Rosales
nodes.summary: The rose order: roses and their fruit-bearing relatives, plus figs, mulberries, hemp, hops, elms and nettles.

nodes.name: Rose family
nodes.summary: A family that fills fruit bowls: apples, pears, plums, cherries, peaches, apricots, almonds, strawberries, raspberries and roses are all close relatives.
facts: Apple, cherry and almond blossoms all have five petals, a family trademark shared with wild roses.
The seeds of many family members, like apples and apricots, contain amygdalin, which can release cyanide.

nodes.name: Apples
nodes.summary: About 35 species of apple and crab apple trees across the Northern Hemisphere. Most wild ones have small, sour fruits.

nodes.name: Wild apple
nodes.summary: The wild forests of Malus sieversii in the Tian Shan mountains are where the apple began. Some of its fruits already taste like modern apples.
facts: Kazakhstan's biggest city, Almaty, takes its name from the Kazakh word for apple.
Bears and wild horses probably ate the biggest, sweetest apples and spread their seeds, giving the species a head start toward big fruit.
These wild apple forests are now threatened and the species is listed as vulnerable.

nodes.name: European crab apple
nodes.summary: A thorny wild apple of European woods with small, mouth-puckeringly sour fruits. It mixed into domestic apples once they reached Europe.
facts: DNA shows modern apples got a large share of their genes from this crab apple, not just from their Central Asian ancestor.

nodes.name: Apple
nodes.summary: The domestic apple: over 7,500 varieties, all descended from wild Tian Shan apples that crossed with European crab apples along the way.
facts: Apple seeds don't grow true: plant a seed and you'll get a completely new kind of apple, usually a sour one. Every named variety is kept going by grafting.
Johnny Appleseed planted apple seeds across the American frontier, but most of his apples were used for cider.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from Malus sieversii in the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan; carried west along the Silk Road, where it hybridised with crab apples. Grafting, known by about 3,800 years ago, let growers copy the best trees.

nodes.name: Granny Smith
nodes.summary: The bright green, tart apple. Every Granny Smith tree in the world is a grafted copy of one lucky seedling.
facts: The seedling probably sprouted from leftover French crab apples she had thrown away.
nodes.origin: Discovered as a chance seedling by Maria Ann Smith in her orchard at Eastwood, Sydney, Australia, in 1868.

nodes.name: Pears
nodes.summary: Pear trees, close cousins of apples, which probably first evolved in the mountains of western China.
facts: Asian pears, or nashi, are round and crunchy like apples but belong to a separate pear species.

nodes.name: European pear
nodes.summary: The juicy, bell-shaped pear of Europe and the Americas. Unusually, it ripens best after picking.
facts: Pears ripen from the inside out, so a pear that's soft on the outside may already be mushy in the middle.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from wild pears of Europe and western Asia (such as Pyrus pyraster and Pyrus caucasica) about 3,000 years ago; the ancient Greeks and Romans grew many varieties.

nodes.name: Stone fruits
nodes.summary: The genus Prunus: peaches, plums, cherries, apricots and almonds. Their fruits are drupes, with a hard stone around a single seed.
facts: An almond is the seed inside the stone of a fruit very like a peach.

nodes.name: Peach
nodes.summary: Fuzzy, juicy stone fruit from China. Fossil peach stones 2.6 million years old show the fruit existed long before people.
facts: Fossil peach pits from Kunming, China, look almost identical to modern ones, though humans hadn't evolved yet.
In Chinese tradition the peach is a symbol of long life.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in the Yangtze River valley of China at least 7,500 years ago; it reached Europe via Persia, which is why its scientific name means 'Persian'.

nodes.name: Nectarine
nodes.summary: A peach without fuzz. A single gene change makes the skin smooth, and nectarine and peach trees sometimes sprout from each other's seeds.
facts: A peach tree can grow a branch that makes nectarines, and vice versa.
nodes.origin: Arose as a natural mutation of the peach, probably in China, more than 2,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Wild almond
nodes.summary: Wild almond trees of the dry hills of Western and Central Asia. Their nuts are bitter and full of amygdalin, which turns into deadly cyanide.
facts: Eating a few dozen wild bitter almonds could kill an adult.

nodes.name: Almond
nodes.summary: Sweet almonds exist because of a single mutation that switched off the bitter poison. Early farmers spotted and planted those rare sweet trees.
facts: A 2019 study found the 'sweet kernel' mutation in a gene called bHLH2 that blocks amygdalin production.
California grows about 80% of the world's almonds, and their bloom needs more than two million rented beehives.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in the Near East (the Levant) about 5,000–6,000 years ago from rare sweet-kernelled trees; spread around the Mediterranean.

nodes.name: Cherry plum
nodes.summary: A small wild plum from south-east Europe and western Asia with cherry-sized red or yellow fruits. It is thought to be one parent of the European plum.

nodes.name: Sloe (blackthorn)
nodes.summary: A thorny hedge shrub of Europe with tiny, sour, blue-black fruits. Probably the other parent of the European plum.
facts: Sloes are famous for flavouring sloe gin.

nodes.name: European plum
nodes.summary: The plum of prunes and damsons, with six sets of chromosomes. It probably formed when cherry plums crossed with sloes.
facts: Prunes are just dried plums.
Chinese plums are a different species, Prunus salicina.
nodes.origin: Probably arose in the Caucasus region where cherry plum and sloe overlap; well established by Roman times.

nodes.name: Wild cherry
nodes.summary: A tall forest tree of Europe and western Asia with small, dark, bittersweet cherries. Birds love them and spread the stones.
facts: Its scientific name 'avium' means 'of the birds'.

nodes.name: Sweet cherry
nodes.summary: Big, sweet, dark cherries selected from wild cherry trees. Sour cherries, used in pies, are a separate hybrid species.
facts: Japan's famous cherry blossom trees are ornamental Prunus hybrids that make tiny, sour fruit.
nodes.origin: Cultivated around the Black Sea and Asia Minor by ancient times; the Romans spread cherry growing across their empire.

nodes.name: Apricot
nodes.summary: A golden, velvety stone fruit. Its scientific name means 'Armenian', but it was actually domesticated in Central Asia and China.
facts: Apricot kernels contain amygdalin, like bitter almonds.
Turkey grows more apricots than any other country, most of them dried.
nodes.origin: Domesticated separately in Central Asia and in China, thousands of years ago; reached Europe via Armenia and Persia.

nodes.name: Strawberries
nodes.summary: Low plants that spread by runners. A strawberry's 'seeds' on the outside are actually its true fruits, called achenes.
facts: An average strawberry carries about 200 of these tiny fruits on its surface.
Botanically, a strawberry isn't a berry at all, but a banana is.

nodes.name: Woodland strawberry
nodes.summary: The tiny, intensely flavoured wild strawberry of Europe's woods. It was the strawberry people picked and grew for centuries before the garden strawberry existed.
facts: Garden strawberries have eight sets of chromosomes, and one of those sets came from an ancestor of this little species.

nodes.name: Virginia strawberry
nodes.summary: A wild North American strawberry with small, bright red, very tasty fruit. Colonists sent it back to Europe in the 1600s.

nodes.name: Chilean strawberry
nodes.summary: A strawberry from the Pacific coast of South America with big, pale, firm fruit. The Mapuche people grew it long before Europeans arrived.
facts: In 1714 a French officer and spy, Amédée-François Frézier, carried five Chilean strawberry plants home; by chance, they were all female.

nodes.name: Garden strawberry
nodes.summary: The modern strawberry: an accidental hybrid of a North American and a South American wild strawberry, born in French gardens.
facts: Its name 'ananassa' means pineapple-like, after its fragrance.
The two wild parents grew 8,000 km apart and only met because humans carried them to Europe.
nodes.origin: Arose around 1750 in Brittany, France, when female Chilean strawberries planted near Virginia strawberries were pollinated by them; botanist Antoine Duchesne worked out its parentage in 1766.

nodes.name: Brambles
nodes.summary: Raspberries, blackberries and their thorny cousins. Each berry is really a cluster of tiny juicy drupelets, each with its own seed.

nodes.name: Raspberry
nodes.summary: A red bramble fruit that comes off its core when picked, leaving a hollow cup.
facts: An average raspberry is made of about 100 drupelets.
nodes.origin: Gathered from the wild for thousands of years; cultivated in European gardens from the Middle Ages onwards.

nodes.name: Blackberry
nodes.summary: The thorny bramble of hedges and wastelands. Unlike a raspberry, a blackberry keeps its core when picked.
facts: Many blackberries make seeds without sex, so they form hundreds of near-identical 'microspecies'.

nodes.name: Loganberry
nodes.summary: A deep red blackberry–raspberry hybrid that appeared by accident in a Californian garden.
facts: Loganberries were later crossed again to make boysenberries.
nodes.origin: Arose in 1881 in the garden of Judge James Harvey Logan in Santa Cruz, California, from a cross between a blackberry and a raspberry.

nodes.name: Roses
nodes.summary: Thorny shrubs with famously fragrant flowers. Thousands of garden varieties come from a handful of wild species from Asia, Europe and the Middle East.
facts: Rose fossils from Colorado are about 35 million years old.
Strictly, rose 'thorns' are prickles: outgrowths of the skin, not modified branches.
In World War II, British volunteers collected rose hips to make vitamin C syrup.
nodes.origin: Cultivated in China, Persia and around the Mediterranean for thousands of years; modern repeat-flowering roses come from crossing Chinese and European roses in the 1800s.

nodes.name: Figs
nodes.summary: About 850 species of fig trees and vines in the mulberry family, including banyans and strangler figs. Their 'fruit' is really a hollow bundle of tiny flowers turned inward.
facts: Most fig species are pollinated by their own species of tiny fig wasp that crawls inside the fig.
Strangler figs start life on top of another tree and slowly wrap and replace it.

nodes.name: Common fig
nodes.summary: A sweet Mediterranean fruit that may be the first plant ever domesticated, a thousand years before wheat.
facts: Many fig varieties grown today don't need fig wasps at all; their fruits develop without pollination.
nodes.origin: Charred figs from Gilgal, in the Jordan Valley, about 11,400 years old, came from seedless trees that can only be kept going by people planting cuttings.

nodes.name: Gourd family
nodes.summary: Climbing and creeping vines with big fruits: pumpkins, squashes, melons, watermelons, cucumbers and gourds.
facts: Bottle gourds were among the first plants people grew, used as containers before pottery.

nodes.name: Kordofan melon
nodes.summary: A wild melon from the Kordofan region of Sudan with pale, non-bitter flesh. DNA shows it is the closest wild relative of the watermelon.

nodes.name: Watermelon
nodes.summary: A giant, juicy fruit that is about 92% water. Farmers turned a pale, hard melon into today's sweet, red-fleshed fruit.
facts: Watermelon seeds were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun.
Seedless watermelons are made by crossing normal plants with plants that have doubled chromosomes, giving sterile offspring.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in north-east Africa, probably Sudan, at least 4,000–5,000 years ago; a 4,300-year-old Egyptian tomb painting shows a striped watermelon.

nodes.name: Melons and cucumbers
nodes.summary: The genus of melons and cucumbers, with wild relatives in Africa, Asia and Australia.

nodes.name: Melon
nodes.summary: Cantaloupe, honeydew and many other melons are all one species, domesticated more than once.
facts: The cantaloupe is named after Cantalupo, a former papal estate near Rome.
nodes.origin: Domesticated at least twice from wild melons: once in Africa and once in India, several thousand years ago.

nodes.name: Cucumber
nodes.summary: A crisp, watery fruit we eat as a vegetable. Its wild ancestors from the Himalayan foothills are bitter.
facts: The Roman emperor Tiberius reportedly ate cucumbers every day, grown in movable beds wheeled into the sun.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in India, in the foothills of the Himalayas, at least 3,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Squashes
nodes.summary: Pumpkins and squashes of the Americas. Wild squashes are bitter and were spread by mammoths and mastodons, which didn't mind.
facts: After the big mammals died out, wild squashes might have disappeared too if humans hadn't started growing them.

nodes.name: Pumpkin
nodes.summary: One of the first crops in the Americas. Pumpkins, zucchini, acorn squash and many ornamental gourds all belong to this one species.
facts: The first jack-o'-lanterns in Ireland and Scotland were carved from turnips, not pumpkins.
Giant pumpkins can weigh over 1,000 kg.
nodes.origin: Seeds about 10,000 years old from Guilá Naquitz cave in Oaxaca, Mexico, are among the oldest evidence of farming in the Americas.

nodes.name: Zucchini (courgette)
nodes.summary: A squash eaten young and tender. It is a summer squash variety of the same species as pumpkins.
facts: Its big yellow flowers are also eaten, often stuffed and fried.
nodes.origin: Developed in northern Italy, probably near Milan, in the late 1800s from squashes brought from the Americas.

nodes.name: Mallow family
nodes.summary: Hibiscus and its relatives, including cacao, cotton, okra, durian, baobab and linden trees.
facts: Marshmallows were originally made from the root of the marsh mallow plant.

nodes.name: Cacao
nodes.summary: A small rainforest tree whose bitter seeds become chocolate. Its flowers and pods grow straight out of the trunk.
facts: The Aztecs used cacao beans as money.
Its tiny flowers are pollinated by midges smaller than a pinhead.
Theobroma means 'food of the gods'.
nodes.origin: First used about 5,300 years ago by the Mayo-Chinchipe people of the upper Amazon in Ecuador; later cultivated in Mesoamerica, where the Maya and Aztecs made chocolate drinks.

nodes.name: Cotton
nodes.summary: Shrubs whose seeds are wrapped in fluffy fibres. Cotton was domesticated four separate times on different continents.
facts: The cotton in most T-shirts comes from a species formed 1–2 million years ago, when seeds of an African-Asian cotton drifted across the ocean and crossed with an American one.
A cotton fibre is a single plant cell that can be over 3 cm long.
nodes.origin: Domesticated independently in South Asia, Africa/Arabia, Mesoamerica and South America; cotton threads from Pakistan are over 7,000 years old.

nodes.name: Sapindales
nodes.summary: An order rich in fruit and fragrance: citrus, mango, cashew, pistachio, lychee, maple, mahogany and frankincense.
facts: Maple syrup and lemonade both come from plants of this order.

nodes.name: Citrus family
nodes.summary: The rue family, aromatic trees and herbs with oil glands dotting their leaves and fruit peel. Includes all citrus fruits and curry leaf.
facts: Hold a citrus leaf up to the light and you'll see tiny see-through dots: oil glands.

nodes.name: Citrus
nodes.summary: The genus of oranges, lemons, limes and grapefruits. Almost all supermarket citrus are hybrids of just a few wild ancestors.
facts: Citrus originated about 8 million years ago in the south-east foothills of the Himalayas.
The 'pure' ancestral species are citron, pomelo, mandarin and a few papedas; nearly everything else is a mix of them.

nodes.name: Citron
nodes.summary: A big, knobbly, thick-skinned citrus that is mostly peel. It was the first citrus to reach the Mediterranean, and it's a parent of lemons and limes.
facts: Buddha's hand is a citron whose fruit splits into finger-like segments.
The etrog used in the Jewish festival of Sukkot is a citron.
nodes.origin: Native to north-east India and nearby regions; carried west to Persia and the Mediterranean by around 300 BC.

nodes.name: Pomelo
nodes.summary: The largest citrus fruit, up to the size of a basketball. It's a mild, sweet ancestor of oranges and grapefruits.
facts: Pomelo is the 'big' half of both the orange and the grapefruit family tree.
nodes.origin: Native to Southeast Asia and southern China, where it has been grown for thousands of years.

nodes.name: Mandarin
nodes.summary: Small, sweet, easy-to-peel citrus native to southern China. It's one of the founding ancestors of most citrus fruits we eat.
facts: Tangerines and satsumas are types of mandarin.
Many 'mandarins' sold today carry a little pomelo DNA from ancient crosses.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in southern China; wild mandarins still grow in the Mangshan mountains of Hunan.

nodes.name: Papeda (Micrantha)
nodes.summary: A small, sour wild citrus from the Philippines. Few people have heard of it, but it is a parent of the key lime.

nodes.name: Sweet orange
nodes.summary: The world's most grown citrus. It is a mandarin–pomelo hybrid, then crossed back to mandarin, and all its varieties descend from one ancestral tree through bud mutations.
facts: In Greek, Arabic, Turkish and several other languages the word for orange is based on 'Portugal'.
In English, the colour was named after the fruit, not the other way round.
nodes.origin: Arose in southern China from crosses between mandarins and pomelos; Portuguese traders brought improved sweet oranges to Europe in the 1500s.

nodes.name: Sour orange
nodes.summary: A bitter, sour orange used for Seville marmalade and perfume. It's a direct pomelo × mandarin cross, and a parent of the lemon.
facts: Neroli perfume oil is distilled from its flowers.
nodes.origin: Formed in South-east Asia or southern China from pomelo and mandarin; Arab traders spread it to the Mediterranean around the 10th century.

nodes.name: Lemon
nodes.summary: A sour, juicy hybrid of the citron and the sour orange. Its acid and vitamin C made it famous at sea.
facts: In 1747 ship's surgeon James Lind showed that citrus cured scurvy, in one of the first controlled medical trials.
nodes.origin: Arose in north-east India, Myanmar or southern China; reached the Mediterranean around the time of the Roman Empire and spread widely with Arab traders.

nodes.name: Grapefruit
nodes.summary: An 18th-century accident in Barbados: a pomelo crossed with a sweet orange. It's named for growing in grape-like clusters.
facts: Grapefruit can make some medicines dangerously strong, because its chemicals block a gut enzyme that breaks drugs down.
Barbados lists it among its 'Seven Wonders'.
nodes.origin: Born in Barbados in the 1700s, where pomelos and sweet oranges brought from Asia grew side by side; first described in 1750 as the 'forbidden fruit'.

nodes.name: Key lime
nodes.summary: A small, fragrant, seedy lime. It's a citron crossed with a little-known wild papeda from the Philippines.
facts: It's the star of the American dessert key lime pie.
nodes.origin: Arose in South-east Asia; carried across the world by traders and grown in the Florida Keys from the 1800s, giving it its name.

nodes.name: Persian lime
nodes.summary: The large, seedless supermarket lime. It is a cross of the key lime and the lemon.
facts: It has three sets of chromosomes, which is why it has no seeds.
nodes.origin: Probably arose in Persia (Iran) or nearby; became the main commercial lime in the 20th century.

nodes.name: Clementine
nodes.summary: A small, sweet, seedless mandarin-type fruit that is a cross of a mandarin and a sweet orange.
nodes.origin: Found in 1902 by Brother Clément Rodier in the garden of an orphanage at Misserghin, Algeria.

nodes.name: Cashew family
nodes.summary: Mango, cashew and pistachio, and also poison ivy. Many members contain urushiol, an oil that causes itchy rashes.
facts: Mango skin can give a poison-ivy-like rash to very sensitive people.

nodes.name: Mango
nodes.summary: A juicy, fragrant tropical fruit and the national fruit of India, Pakistan and the Philippines.
facts: The paisley pattern is called 'ambi' or 'kairi' in Hindi, meaning mango.
Mango trees can live and bear fruit for over 100 years.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in South Asia (India and Myanmar region) about 4,000 years ago; Buddhist monks and later traders carried it across Asia, and the Portuguese took it to Africa and Brazil.

nodes.name: Cashew
nodes.summary: A Brazilian tree whose nut hangs below a juicy 'cashew apple'. The shell contains a caustic oil, so the nuts are always heated before sale.
facts: Each cashew apple has only one nut, growing on the outside.
The cashew apple is eaten and made into juice in Brazil and India.
nodes.origin: Native to north-eastern Brazil; Portuguese colonists carried it to India and East Africa in the 1500s, which are now major producers.

nodes.name: Brassicales
nodes.summary: Plants armed with mustard oils: cabbages, mustards, capers, papaya and nasturtiums. Chewing their tissue sets off a sharp-tasting chemical defence.
facts: The 'bite' of mustard, wasabi and horseradish comes from a defence called the 'mustard oil bomb'.

nodes.name: Papaya
nodes.summary: A fast-growing, soft-stemmed tropical plant with sweet orange fruit. Surprisingly, it's a relative of cabbages and mustard.
facts: Its enzyme papain is used to tenderise meat.
A genetically engineered 'Rainbow' papaya, released in 1998, saved Hawaii's papaya farms from ringspot virus.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in southern Mexico and Central America; spread across the tropics by Spanish and Portuguese sailors in the 1500s.

nodes.name: Cabbage family
nodes.summary: Mustards and crucifers: cabbages, turnips, radishes, mustard, rocket, wasabi and the lab plant Arabidopsis. Their four petals form a cross.
facts: Thale cress (Arabidopsis), a tiny weed of this family, was the first plant to have its genome fully sequenced, in 2000.

nodes.name: Brassicas
nodes.summary: A genus that people have sculpted into an amazing range of vegetables: cabbages, turnips, mustards, rapeseed and more.
facts: The 'Triangle of U' (1935) showed how three Brassica species crossed to form three new ones, including rapeseed.

nodes.name: Wild cabbage
nodes.summary: A tough, leafy plant of Atlantic and Mediterranean sea cliffs. Broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, kale, kohlrabi and Brussels sprouts are all this one species.
facts: Wild cabbage still grows on the chalk cliffs of southern England, including the White Cliffs of Dover.
Farmers made each vegetable by selecting a different part: leaves, buds, stems or flowers.

nodes.name: Kale
nodes.summary: The cabbage selected for big, loose leaves, the closest of the cabbage vegetables to its wild ancestor.
facts: Kale was one of the most common green vegetables in Europe until the Middle Ages.
nodes.origin: Grown by ancient Greeks and Romans in the Mediterranean more than 2,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Cabbage
nodes.summary: Leaves wrapped into a tight ball: a cabbage head is really one giant bud.
facts: Captain Cook fed his sailors sauerkraut, fermented cabbage, to help prevent scurvy.
nodes.origin: Tight-headed cabbages were developed in Europe in the Middle Ages, around 1,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Broccoli
nodes.summary: The cabbage selected for thick clusters of green flower buds. Each 'tree' is a bunch of unopened flowers.
facts: 'Broccoli' comes from the Italian 'brocco', meaning sprout or shoot.
If you don't harvest it, broccoli bursts into small yellow flowers.
nodes.origin: Developed in Italy, probably in Roman times, and spread through Europe from there.

nodes.name: Cauliflower
nodes.summary: A tight white 'curd' of stunted flower buds. Genetics shows cauliflower was bred from broccoli.
facts: Mark Twain called cauliflower 'nothing but cabbage with a college education'.
Farmers tie leaves over the head to keep it white; orange and purple varieties exist too.
nodes.origin: Developed from broccoli-like plants in the eastern Mediterranean in the Middle Ages, then refined in Italy and northern Europe.

nodes.name: Romanesco
nodes.summary: A lime-green cauliflower whose florets form spiralling fractals: every bump is made of smaller bumps of the same shape.
facts: The number of spirals on a Romanesco head is usually a Fibonacci number.
nodes.origin: Grown near Rome, Italy, at least since the 16th century.

nodes.name: Brussels sprouts
nodes.summary: Tiny cabbages that grow up a tall stalk: each sprout is a swollen side bud.
facts: Some people taste sprouts as much more bitter because of their version of a bitter-taste gene, TAS2R38.
Since the 1990s, breeders have produced milder sprouts by reducing bitter compounds.
nodes.origin: Developed in what is now Belgium, near Brussels, probably by the 1500s.

nodes.name: Kohlrabi
nodes.summary: A cabbage bred for its swollen, ball-shaped stem, which looks a bit like an alien turnip.
facts: Its German name means 'cabbage turnip'.
nodes.origin: Developed in northern Europe, probably by the 1500s.

nodes.name: Spurge family
nodes.summary: A huge family, many with milky, often poisonous sap: rubber trees, castor beans, poinsettias, cactus-like spurges and cassava.
facts: Natural rubber comes from the latex of the rubber tree, a member of this family.

nodes.name: Cassava
nodes.summary: A starchy root that feeds hundreds of millions of people in the tropics. Raw cassava contains compounds that release cyanide, so it must be properly processed.
facts: Tapioca pearls are made from cassava starch.
Cassava survives drought and poor soils where few other crops can grow.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in the south-western Amazon, in Brazil, roughly 8,000–10,000 years ago; Portuguese traders took it to Africa, now the biggest producer.

nodes.name: Asterids
nodes.summary: A huge branch of eudicots with tube-shaped flowers, including sunflowers, tomatoes, potatoes, coffee, olives, mint, carrots and blueberries.

nodes.name: Ericales
nodes.summary: A varied order that includes blueberries, cranberries, kiwifruit, tea, persimmons, Brazil nuts and rhododendrons.

nodes.name: Blueberries and cranberries
nodes.summary: Shrubs of the heath family that love acidic soils: blueberries, cranberries, bilberries and lingonberries.

nodes.name: Highbush blueberry
nodes.summary: A North American shrub that became a crop only about a century ago, making it one of the youngest domesticated fruits.
facts: The blue colour isn't just pigment: a waxy coating of tiny crystals scatters blue light.
Inside, most blueberries are pale green, not blue.
nodes.origin: Domesticated between 1908 and 1916 in New Jersey by USDA botanist Frederick Coville and farmer Elizabeth White, who sold the first commercial crop in 1916.

nodes.name: Cranberry
nodes.summary: A low, creeping North American shrub with tart red berries that contain pockets of air.
facts: Farmers flood the fields at harvest time and the cranberries float to the surface.
Good cranberries bounce! Growers once sorted them with 'bounce boards'.
nodes.origin: Indigenous peoples of north-eastern North America used wild cranberries; cultivation began around 1816 when Henry Hall of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, planted them in bogs.

nodes.name: Chinese gooseberry
nodes.summary: A wild climbing vine from the forests of central and southern China with small, fuzzy, green-fleshed fruits.
facts: Chinese people gathered it from the wild for centuries but rarely farmed it.

nodes.name: Kiwifruit
nodes.summary: The fuzzy brown fruit with bright green flesh, bred in New Zealand from Chinese gooseberry seeds and renamed for marketing.
facts: Kiwifruit has more vitamin C than an orange, weight for weight.
Almost all green kiwifruit sold are the 'Hayward' variety, bred by New Zealander Hayward Wright in the 1920s.
nodes.origin: Seeds were brought from Yichang, China, to New Zealand in 1904 by school principal Isabel Fraser; the first fruits ripened in 1910, and exporters renamed it 'kiwifruit' in 1959.

nodes.name: Tea
nodes.summary: An evergreen camellia shrub. Green, black, oolong and white tea all come from the leaves of this one plant, just processed differently.
facts: Tea plants make caffeine as a natural insecticide.
After water, tea is the most consumed drink in the world.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in south-western China (Yunnan region) thousands of years ago; tea leaves were found in a Chinese emperor's tomb about 2,100 years old.

nodes.name: Coffee family
nodes.summary: The madder family, one of the largest plant families, with coffee, gardenias and the quinine tree whose bark fought malaria.

nodes.name: Coffee plants
nodes.summary: About 130 species of coffee shrubs from Africa, Madagascar and Asia. Only two are grown on a large scale.
facts: Coffee 'beans' are seeds inside red fruits called coffee cherries.

nodes.name: Robusta coffee
nodes.summary: A tough, high-yielding coffee from the lowland forests of central and western Africa. It has about twice as much caffeine as arabica.
nodes.origin: Cultivated from the late 1800s, especially after coffee leaf rust devastated arabica farms in Asia; Vietnam is now its biggest grower.

nodes.name: Coffea eugenioides
nodes.summary: A wild, low-caffeine coffee from the highlands of East Africa. It is one of the two parents of arabica coffee.

nodes.name: Arabica coffee
nodes.summary: The world's favourite coffee. It formed naturally in Ethiopia's forests when robusta and Coffea eugenioides crossed and doubled their chromosomes.
facts: A famous legend says an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi discovered coffee when his goats got frisky after eating the berries.
Arabica has very little genetic diversity, which makes it vulnerable to diseases like coffee leaf rust.
nodes.origin: The hybrid arose about 600,000 years ago in Ethiopia; coffee was first cultivated and brewed in Yemen by the 1400s, then spread through the Ottoman world and Europe.

nodes.name: Olive family
nodes.summary: Olives, ash trees, lilacs, jasmine and forsythia.

nodes.name: Wild olive
nodes.summary: The spiny, small-fruited wild olive of Mediterranean scrub. Its little oily fruits are spread by birds.

nodes.name: Olive
nodes.summary: An evergreen tree that can live for thousands of years, grown for olive oil and cured olives. Raw olives are far too bitter to eat.
facts: Winners at the ancient Olympic Games were crowned with olive wreaths.
Some olive trees around the Mediterranean are thought to be over 2,000 years old.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from wild olives in the Levant about 7,000 years ago; olive oil traces in 7,000-year-old pottery from Galilee are among the earliest evidence.

nodes.name: Solanales
nodes.summary: The nightshade order: tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, tobacco, plus morning glories and sweet potatoes.

nodes.name: Nightshade family
nodes.summary: A family of food plants and poisons: tomatoes, potatoes, chili peppers and eggplants, but also deadly nightshade, mandrake and tobacco.
facts: A 52-million-year-old fossil from Patagonia is a tomatillo-like fruit inside its papery husk.
Deadly nightshade is called belladonna, 'beautiful lady', because women once used its juice to widen their pupils.

nodes.name: Solanum
nodes.summary: One of the biggest plant genera, with over 1,000 species, including tomato, potato and eggplant.

nodes.name: Currant tomato
nodes.summary: A wild tomato from the coasts of Ecuador and Peru with tasty red fruits the size of a pea. It is the wild ancestor of the tomato.

nodes.name: Tomato
nodes.summary: Botanically a berry, legally a vegetable. Tomatoes went from pea-sized wild fruits to giant beefsteaks.
facts: Many Europeans feared tomatoes were poisonous for about 200 years.
In 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled that the tomato is a vegetable, for tax purposes.
A tomato has more genes than a human: about 35,000 compared to our roughly 20,000.
nodes.origin: Partly domesticated as a cherry-like tomato in Ecuador and northern Peru, then fully domesticated in Mexico; the Aztecs called it tomatl. Spanish explorers brought it to Europe in the 1500s.

nodes.name: Wild potato
nodes.summary: Small, bitter wild potatoes of the high Andes. The closest wild relative of the cultivated potato is a Peruvian species, Solanum candolleanum.
facts: The whole potato lineage began about 9 million years ago with a hybrid between an ancient tomato-like plant and a relative called Etuberosum, which is how it got tubers.

nodes.name: Potato
nodes.summary: The world's most important root-type crop. In the Andes there are thousands of varieties in every colour.
facts: The Irish Potato Famine (1845–1852), caused by potato blight, killed about a million people.
Andean people invented chuño, freeze-dried potatoes that keep for years.
In 1995 the potato became the first food plant grown in space.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in the Andes of southern Peru and north-western Bolivia, near Lake Titicaca, about 7,000–10,000 years ago; reached Europe via Spain in the late 1500s.

nodes.name: Eggplant (aubergine)
nodes.summary: A glossy purple vegetable domesticated in Asia. Its English name comes from early European varieties that were small, white and egg-shaped.
facts: The name 'aubergine' travelled from Sanskrit through Persian and Arabic to Catalan and French.
nodes.origin: Domesticated from wild Solanum insanum in South and South-east Asia, probably India and also China, more than 2,000 years ago.

nodes.name: Peppers
nodes.summary: Chili and bell peppers. Their spicy capsaicin keeps mammals from eating the fruits, but birds can't feel the burn and spread the seeds.
facts: Capsaicin triggers the same nerve receptor that senses heat, which is why chili feels 'hot'.

nodes.name: Chiltepin
nodes.summary: A wild pepper with tiny, fiery, round red fruits eaten by birds. Called the 'mother of all peppers', it's the wild ancestor of most chili varieties.
facts: It is the official native pepper of Texas.

nodes.name: Chili pepper
nodes.summary: Jalapeño, cayenne, paprika and sweet bell peppers are all the same species, bred in Mexico from fiery wild chiltepins.
facts: Before the 1500s, Indian, Thai and Sichuan cooking had no chili at all.
Columbus called them 'peppers' because their heat reminded him of black pepper, an unrelated plant.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in Mexico at least 6,000 years ago; after 1492 Portuguese and Spanish traders spread chili to Africa, India, Thailand and China within a few decades.

nodes.name: Tobacco
nodes.summary: A nightshade from the Americas whose leaves are loaded with nicotine. It formed when two wild Nicotiana species crossed and doubled their chromosomes.
facts: Nicotine is the plant's natural insecticide.
Tobacco mosaic virus, found in the 1890s, was the first virus ever discovered.
nodes.origin: Cultivated by Indigenous peoples of the Americas for thousands of years for ceremony and medicine; spread worldwide after the 1500s.

nodes.name: Sweet potato
nodes.summary: A sweet root from the morning glory family, only a distant cousin of the potato. It is a natural GMO: it carries genes picked up from soil bacteria long ago.
facts: Its DNA contains genes from Agrobacterium bacteria, inserted naturally thousands of years ago.
How it got to Polynesia before Columbus, by human voyagers or floating seeds, is still debated.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in tropical Central or South America at least 5,000 years ago; it reached Polynesia centuries before European explorers.

nodes.name: Carrot family
nodes.summary: Umbrella-flowered plants: carrots, parsnips, celery, parsley, dill, fennel, cumin and coriander, but also deadly poison hemlock.
facts: The philosopher Socrates was executed with a drink of poison hemlock, a member of the carrot family.

nodes.name: Wild carrot
nodes.summary: Queen Anne's lace: a roadside wildflower with lacy white flower umbrellas and a thin, pale, woody root.
facts: Many flower heads have a single dark-red floret in the centre, which may attract insects.

nodes.name: Carrot
nodes.summary: The first cultivated carrots weren't orange: they were purple and yellow.
nodes.origin: Domesticated in Central Asia, around today's Afghanistan and Iran, roughly 1,100 years ago; purple and yellow carrots spread to Europe and China by the 1300s.

nodes.name: Orange carrot
nodes.summary: The orange carrot, rich in beta-carotene, was developed in Europe and became the world standard.
facts: The story that Dutch growers bred orange carrots to honour the House of Orange is a popular legend without solid evidence.
In World War II, Britain spread the myth that carrots gave pilots night vision, to hide the fact that they were using radar.
nodes.origin: Developed in the Netherlands and nearby in the 1500s–1600s from yellow carrots.

nodes.name: Daisy family
nodes.summary: One of the largest plant families, with about 32,000 species. Each 'flower' of a daisy or sunflower is actually hundreds of tiny florets.
facts: Lettuce, artichokes, chamomile, dandelions and sunflowers are all in the daisy family.

nodes.name: Sunflower
nodes.summary: A giant daisy from North America, grown for seeds and oil. Its seeds are arranged in mathematical spirals.
facts: Young sunflowers follow the sun from east to west each day, but mature heads face east, which warms them and attracts more bees.
The seed spirals usually come in Fibonacci numbers, like 34 and 55.
nodes.origin: Domesticated by Native Americans in eastern North America about 4,000–5,000 years ago; became a major oil crop in Russia in the 1800s.
